title: What are the database lock types — Shared (S, read, many allowed concurrently), Exclusive (X, write, only one), and Intent locks (signal an intention to lock at a lower granularity so the engine can check compatibility cheaply) — and what is lock escalation (the engine converting many fine-grained row locks into fewer coarse-grained table/page locks to reduce overhead, at the cost of concurrency)?
shortTitle: Database Lock Types (Shared, Exclusive, Intent) and Lock Escalation

s1_definition.profdef: Database lock types control concurrent access. A Shared lock (S) is for reading and multiple transactions can hold it on the same resource at once; an Exclusive lock (X) is for writing and only one transaction can hold it, blocking all others. Intent locks (IS, IX) are placed on a coarser level (like a table) to signal that a transaction intends to lock finer-grained resources (rows) beneath it, letting the engine check lock compatibility cheaply without scanning every row lock. Lock escalation is the engine automatically converting many fine-grained locks (thousands of row locks) into fewer coarse-grained locks (a page or table lock) to reduce the memory and management overhead of tracking so many locks, at the cost of reduced concurrency.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of National Bank of India's ledger. A shared lock is many auditors reading the same page together — all allowed, since reading doesn't conflict. An exclusive lock is one clerk editing a line while everyone else waits. An intent lock is a note on the cover of the ledger saying "someone inside is about to edit a line," so another person wanting to lock the whole ledger can see the conflict instantly without flipping through every page. Lock escalation is when so many individual lines are locked that the librarian decides it's simpler to just lock the whole ledger — less bookkeeping, but now nobody else can touch any line.
s1_definition.oneliner: Shared (S) locks allow many concurrent readers, Exclusive (X) locks allow one writer, Intent locks (IS/IX) signal fine-grained locking so compatibility is checked cheaply, and lock escalation trades many row locks for a coarse table/page lock to cut overhead at the cost of concurrency.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Database lock types control concurrent access. A Shared lock (S) is for reading and multiple transactions can hold it on the same resource at once; an Exclusive lock (X) is for writing and only one transaction can hold it, blocking all others. Intent locks (IS, IX) are placed on a coarser level (like a table) to signal that a transaction intends to lock finer-grained resources (rows) beneath it, letting the engine check lock compatibility cheaply without scanning every row lock. Lock escalation is the engine automatically converting many fine-grained locks (thousands of row locks) into fewer coarse-grained locks (a page or table lock) to reduce the memory and management overhead of tracking so many locks, at the cost of reduced concurrency.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of National Bank of India's ledger. A shared lock is many auditors reading the same page together — all allowed, since reading doesn't conflict. An exclusive lock is one clerk editing a line while everyone else waits. An intent lock is a note on the cover of the ledger saying "someone inside is about to edit a line," so another person wanting to lock the whole ledger can see the conflict instantly without flipping through every page. Lock escalation is when so many individual lines are locked that the librarian decides it's simpler to just lock the whole ledger — less bookkeeping, but now nobody else can touch any line.

**One line to remember:** Shared (S) locks allow many concurrent readers, Exclusive (X) locks allow one writer, Intent locks (IS/IX) signal fine-grained locking so compatibility is checked cheaply, and lock escalation trades many row locks for a coarse table/page lock to cut overhead at the cost of concurrency.

sections.s2_technical:
Locks coordinate concurrent access so transactions don't corrupt each other's work. A Shared lock (S) is acquired to read a resource and is compatible with other shared locks — many transactions can read the same row or page simultaneously — but it is incompatible with an exclusive lock, so a reader blocks a writer and vice versa. An Exclusive lock (X) is acquired to modify a resource and is incompatible with everything, including other shared locks, so only one transaction may hold it and all other access waits. This S/X compatibility is the core of lock-based concurrency: readers don't block readers, but writers block everyone on that resource.

Intent locks solve a performance problem in multi-granularity locking. Databases lock at different levels — row, page, table — and before a transaction locks a specific row with X, it first places an Intent Exclusive (IX) lock on the containing page and table, and before a shared row lock it places an Intent Shared (IS). The intent lock is a cheap flag at the coarse level that says "a finer lock exists or is coming below me." Its purpose is efficiency: if another transaction wants an exclusive lock on the whole table, the engine only needs to see the table's IX intent lock to know there's a conflict, instead of scanning thousands of individual row locks to check. There is also SIX (shared with intent exclusive). Intent locks don't block ordinary row-level work; they just make table-level compatibility checks O(1).

Lock escalation is the engine's response to holding too many fine-grained locks. Each lock costs memory and management overhead, so when a single transaction accumulates a large number of row locks (SQL Server escalates around 5000 locks on one object, for instance), the engine converts them into a single coarser lock — a page or, more commonly, a whole-table lock. This slashes the bookkeeping overhead, but the cost is concurrency: a table-level X lock now blocks every other transaction from that table, even rows the original transaction never touched. Escalation is why a large `UPDATE` or `DELETE` touching many rows can suddenly block unrelated work. Engines differ: SQL Server does row→table escalation automatically (controllable via `LOCK_ESCALATION` and avoidable by batching), InnoDB primarily does row-level locking with next-key locks and doesn't escalate the same way but can take table locks in some cases, and Oracle uses row-level locks and generally avoids escalation. The senior guidance is to avoid unwanted escalation by keeping transactions small, updating in batches, using good indexes so you lock few rows rather than scanning many, and choosing the right isolation level — and to understand that escalation is a deliberate trade of concurrency for lower overhead that you manage, not a bug.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem — National Bank of India ran a year-end job that updated an interest flag on millions of account rows in one giant transaction. Midway, tellers reported the whole accounts table was blocked and normal operations stalled. The cause was lock escalation: the engine, holding millions of row locks, escalated to a table-level exclusive lock, blocking every other transaction. The fix was to batch the update into chunks so the engine never accumulated enough row locks to escalate, keeping other transactions unblocked. The team also used this to teach S/X compatibility and the role of intent locks.

Our mini-project simulates a lock manager with S, X, and intent locks and compatibility checks, plus an escalation threshold: it shows that many shared reads coexist, an exclusive lock blocks them, intent locks let a table-level request detect a conflict cheaply, and once row locks exceed a threshold the manager escalates to a table lock — then shows how batching avoids escalation.
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: lock requests in various modes and two update strategies — one giant update of three million rows and a batched update of two thousand rows per chunk.

Step 1 — Two shared-lock requests are compared and found compatible, so multiple readers can hold a shared lock on the same resource at once, reflecting that reads do not conflict with reads.

Step 2 — A shared lock held against an exclusive request is incompatible, so a writer must wait for readers, and an exclusive lock held against any request is incompatible, so one writer blocks everyone — this is the S/X core.

Step 3 — Two intent-exclusive requests on a table are compatible, because each merely signals that some child row will be locked, so many transactions can each lock different rows of the same table simultaneously.

Step 4 — An intent-exclusive lock held against a full table exclusive request is incompatible, and crucially the engine detects this conflict just by seeing the table's intent lock, without scanning the thousands of individual row locks beneath it — that is the whole point of intent locks.

Step 5 — The giant update of three million rows exceeds the escalation threshold, so the manager escalates to a single table lock, cutting lock overhead but blocking the entire table, while the batched update of two thousand rows stays below the threshold and keeps row-level locking with high concurrency — showing how batching avoids the stall.

Final output:

```text
-- Lock compatibility --
  S  held, S  requested (two readers)      = true
  S  held, X  requested (reader vs writer) = false
  X  held, S  requested (writer blocks all)= false
  IX held, IX requested (two row-writers)  = true
  IX held, X  requested (table-lock wants) = false   <- intent lock makes this conflict cheap to detect

-- Lock escalation --
  one huge UPDATE (3,000,000 rows): ESCALATED: 3000000 row locks -> 1 TABLE lock (low overhead, blocks whole table)
  batched UPDATE (2,000 rows/chunk): row-level locking: 2000 row locks (high concurrency)  <- stays below threshold, no escalation
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  COMPATIBILITY:
    S + S = OK (many readers)      S + X = conflict (reader vs writer)
    X + anything = conflict         IX + IX = OK (row-writers on different rows)

  INTENT LOCK (multi-granularity):
    table [ IX ]  ← cheap flag: "a row X-lock lives below"
       └─ row [ X ]
    another txn wants table X → sees table IX → conflict detected in O(1)
       (no need to scan every row lock)

  ESCALATION:
    many row locks ──threshold exceeded──▶ ONE table lock
       (↓ overhead, ↓ concurrency)   |   batch updates to stay below threshold
```
sections.s5c_hld:
```text
  ═══ HLD — Multi-Granularity Locking & Escalation ═══

  TABLE  ─── IS / IX / S / X ─── (coarse: intent flags + whole-table locks)
    │
  PAGE   ─── (medium)
    │
  ROW    ─── S / X ─── (fine: high concurrency, many locks = overhead)

  engine tracks each lock (memory cost)
        │ too many fine locks on one object
        ▼
  ESCALATE → single coarse lock  (overhead ↓, concurrency ↓)
  mitigate: batch DML, good indexes, short txns, right isolation level
```
sections.s5d_lld:
```text
  ═══ LLD — Lock Manager ═══

  ┌─ Design Patterns Used ───────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Compatibility Matrix: mode×mode → allowed?                        │
  │ Policy/Threshold: escalation decision rule                        │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─ SOLID ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ S: manager only decides compatibility + escalation               │
  │ O: new mode (SIX) = new matrix entry                             │
  │ D: callers depend on compatible()/maybeEscalate() contract       │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── Lock types ──
  S  (Shared)    : read | many concurrent | blocks X
  X  (Exclusive) : write | one only | blocks everything
  IS (Intent S)  : "will take S on a child row" (coarse flag)
  IX (Intent X)  : "will take X on a child row" → cheap table-level conflict check
  SIX            : shared + intent exclusive

  ── Lock escalation ──
  trigger : too many row locks on one object (e.g. SQL Server ~5000)
  action  : row/page locks → single TABLE lock
  effect  : overhead ↓↓ , concurrency ↓↓ (blocks untouched rows too)
  engines : SQL Server auto-escalates | InnoDB row-level, next-key, rarely | Oracle row-level
  avoid   : batch DML, index predicates, short transactions

  ── Call Chain ──
  1. Demo.main()
  2.   → compatible(S,S)/(S,X)/(X,S)/(IX,IX)/(IX,X)
  3.   → maybeEscalate(3_000_000)  [ESCALATED to table lock]
  4.   → maybeEscalate(2_000)      [row-level, no escalation]
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Database locks coordinate concurrent access, and the three types to know are shared, exclusive, and intent locks. A Shared lock (S) is taken to read a resource and is compatible with other shared locks, so many transactions can read the same row or page at once, but it conflicts with an exclusive lock, so a reader blocks a writer and vice versa. An Exclusive lock (X) is taken to modify a resource and is incompatible with everything including other shared locks, so only one transaction holds it and all other access waits. Intent locks — Intent Shared and Intent Exclusive — are placed at a coarser level like a table before a transaction takes a finer S or X lock on a row beneath it, and their purpose is pure efficiency: they are a cheap flag that lets the engine detect a conflict with a table-level request in constant time by looking at the table's intent lock, instead of scanning thousands of individual row locks.

Lock escalation is the engine automatically converting many fine-grained locks into one coarse-grained lock when a transaction accumulates too many of them, because each lock costs memory and management overhead. SQL Server, for example, escalates around five thousand locks on one object by replacing the row locks with a single table lock. This slashes the bookkeeping cost, but the trade-off is concurrency: a table-level exclusive lock now blocks every other transaction from that table, including rows the escalating transaction never touched. At the National Bank of India a year-end job that updated an interest flag on millions of account rows in one transaction caused exactly this — the engine escalated to a table lock and stalled all teller operations — and we fixed it by batching the update into small chunks so it never accumulated enough row locks to escalate, keeping other transactions unblocked. The senior guidance I state is that escalation is a deliberate overhead-versus-concurrency trade you manage, not a bug, and you avoid unwanted escalation by keeping transactions small, updating in batches, indexing predicates so you lock few rows, and choosing the right isolation level; engines also differ, with SQL Server auto-escalating while InnoDB and Oracle stay primarily row-level. The line I always state is that Shared locks allow many readers, Exclusive locks allow one writer, Intent locks cheaply signal fine-grained locking for fast compatibility checks, and lock escalation trades many row locks for a coarse table lock to cut overhead at the cost of concurrency.
